svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "The emission spectrum of hydrogen."], [1, "An electron excited to a high level falls back down, giving out a photon: \u0394E = hf."], [3, "Falls to n = 2: visible lines \u2014 656 nm red, 486 nm blue-green, 434 and 410 nm violet."], [7.5, "Falls to n = 1: the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet."], [10, "Falls to n = 3: the Paschen series, in the infrared."], [12.5, "The lines converge: the convergence limit gives the ionisation energy."]]
svg.title: The hydrogen emission spectrum
svg.desc: Energy levels of the hydrogen atom with electron transitions down to n = 1 (Lyman, ultraviolet), n = 2 (Balmer, visible lines at 656, 486, 434 and 410 nm) and n = 3 (Paschen, infrared), and the visible line spectrum.
svg.text: Energy levels drawn to scale: Eₙ = −1312 / n² kJ mol⁻¹.

g.data-info: The electron in hydrogen can only have certain energies: Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹. Levels get closer together as n increases.
Transitions down to n = 2 give visible light: 656 nm (red, 3→2), 486 nm (blue-green, 4→2), 434 nm and 410 nm (violet).
Transitions down to n = 1: larger energy gaps, so ultraviolet.
Transitions down to n = 3: smaller gaps, infrared.
Only certain wavelengths appear: evidence that electron energies are quantised. Lines converge at higher frequency.
Where the lines merge: the electron is removed completely. For the Lyman series this gives the ionisation energy of hydrogen, 1312 kJ mol⁻¹.

g.text: so lines in each series converge.
Lyman limit → ionisation energy 1312 kJ mol⁻¹

g.data-info: The energy of each photon equals the energy difference between the two levels; bigger drop = higher frequency, shorter wavelength.
